Let’s go straight to the mechanics — this is a standard **ordinary annuity** (payments at end of each year).

### Given

A = 1,000
i = 8% = 0.08
n = 5

---

## Present Worth (P)

[
P = A \left(\frac{1-(1+i)^{-n}}{i}\right)
]

[
(1.08)^5 = 1.46933 \Rightarrow (1.08)^{-5} = 0.68058
]

[
P = 1000 \left(\frac{1 - 0.68058}{0.08}\right)
= 1000 (3.9927)
]

[
\boxed{P \approx $3,992.71}
]

---

## Future Worth (F)

[
F = A \left(\frac{(1+i)^n - 1}{i}\right)
]

[
F = 1000 \left(\frac{1.46933 - 1}{0.08}\right)
= 1000 (5.8666)
]

[
\boxed{F \approx $5,866.60}
]

---

## Final Results

| Measure         | Value         |
| --------------- | ------------- |
| Present Worth P | **$3,992.71** |
| Future Worth F  | **$5,866.60** |

### Quick logic check

* Total paid = $5,000
* Discounted to today = $3,992 → time value erodes ~$1,008
* Compounded forward = $5,866 → interest adds ~$866

Different directions, same economic reality.

If you want this shown using factor tables instead of formulas (P/A and F/A), say so.

submissions.solution:
Let’s break it into the **two components** they’re testing you on:

1. uniform series, 2) arithmetic gradient.

---

## 1. Present worth of the base uniform series

Base payment:

* (A = 200) each year
* (n = 6) years
* (i = 10%)

Present worth of a uniform series:

[
P_A = A \left(\frac{1 - (1+i)^{-n}}{i}\right)
]

We already know:
[
(1.10)^6 = 1.771561,\quad (1.10)^{-6} = 0.56447393
]

So:

[
P_A = 200 \cdot \frac{1 - 0.56447393}{0.10}
= 200 \cdot \frac{0.43552607}{0.10}
= 200 \cdot 4.3552607
\approx 871.05
]

So:

[
\boxed{P_A \approx $871.05}
]

---

## 2. Present worth of the arithmetic gradient

Gradient starts in **year 2** and increases by (G = 100) each year:

* Year 2: +100 → total 200 + 100
* Year 3: +200
* Year 4: +300
* Year 5: +400
* Year 6: +500

So the **extra (gradient) part** is:

[
\begin{array}{c|c}
\text{Year} & \text{Extra amount (only gradient)} \
\hline
2 & 100 \
3 & 200 \
4 & 300 \
5 & 400 \
6 & 500 \
\end{array}
]

Discount each to present (year 0):

* Year 2: (100 / 1.10 = 90.91)
* Year 3: (200 / 1.10^2 = 200/1.21 = 165.29)
* Year 4: (300 / 1.10^3 = 300/1.331 = 225.42)
* Year 5: (400 / 1.10^4 = 400/1.4641 = 273.29)
* Year 6: (500 / 1.10^5 = 500/1.61051 = 310.64)

Sum:

[
P_G \approx 90.91 + 165.29 + 225.42 + 273.29 + 310.64 \approx 1{,}065.26
]

So:

[
\boxed{P_G \approx $1{,}065.26}
]

---

## 3. Total present worth (P_T)

[
P_T = P_A + P_G \approx 871.05 + 1{,}065.26 = 1{,}936.31
]

[
\boxed{P_T \approx $1{,}936.31}
]

---

## 4. Total equivalent annual series (A_T)

Now convert that total present worth back to a **single uniform annual amount** over 6 years at 10%.

Use the **capital recovery factor**:

[
A = P \cdot \frac{i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1}
]

We already have ((1.10)^6 = 1.771561), so:

[
\text{CRF} = \frac{0.10 \cdot 1.771561}{1.771561 - 1}
= \frac{0.1771561}{0.771561}
\approx 0.22961
]

Thus:

[
A_T = P_T \cdot \text{CRF}
\approx 1{,}936.31 \cdot 0.22961
\approx 444.59
]

[
\boxed{A_T \approx $444.59 \text{ per year}}
]

---

### Final answers

* **Total present worth:**
  [
  \boxed{P_T \approx $1{,}936.31}
  ]

* **Equivalent uniform annual series (years 1–6):**
  [
  \boxed{A_T \approx $444.59 \text{ per year}}
  ]

If you want, we can next rewrite this using pure factor notation:
(P_T = 200(P/A,10%,6) + 100(P/G,10%,6)), then (A_T = P_T(A/P,10%,6)), which is how exam keys usually present it.

submissions.solution:
Alright, this one is just a shifted annuity. The only “hard” part is keeping the time index straight.

You have a uniform series of **$500 from year 4 to year 9** (6 payments) at **8%**, and you want **P₀** using four methods.

Let’s compute the value once (cleanly), then show how each method reaches the *same* number.

---

### Precomputed factors (at i = 8%)

We’ll use these repeatedly:

* ((1.08)^3 = 1.259712 \Rightarrow (P/F,8%,3) = 1/(1.259712) \approx 0.7938)
* ((1.08)^6 = 1.586874 \Rightarrow (1.08)^{-6} \approx 0.6302)

**P/A factor (8%, 6):**

[
P/A = \frac{1 - (1.08)^{-6}}{0.08}
= \frac{1 - 0.6302}{0.08}
= \frac{0.3698}{0.08}
\approx 4.6229
]

**F/A factor (8%, 6):**

[
F/A = \frac{(1.08)^6 - 1}{0.08}
= \frac{1.586874 - 1}{0.08}
= \frac{0.586874}{0.08}
\approx 7.3359
]

**(P/F,8%,9):**

[
(1.08)^9 \approx 1.9990 \Rightarrow (P/F,8%,9) \approx \frac{1}{1.9990} \approx 0.5002
]

We’ll reuse these.

---

## Method (d) – Easiest and most standard

Uniform series from year 4–9 → its “present” is naturally at **year 3**.

1. **Present at year 3 (P₃)** using P/A:

[
P_3 = 500 \cdot (P/A, 8%, 6)
= 500 \cdot 4.6229
\approx 2{,}311.45
]

2. **Discount to year 0:**

[
P_0 = P_3 \cdot (P/F, 8%, 3)
= 2{,}311.45 \cdot 0.7938
\approx 1{,}835 \text{ (rounded)}
]

So:

[
\boxed{P_0 \approx $1{,}835}
]

This is the number all methods must match.

---

## Method (a): Direct summation to year 0

Cash flows are at years 4,5,6,7,8,9:

[
P_0 = 500\left[
\frac{1}{(1.08)^4}

* \frac{1}{(1.08)^5}
* \frac{1}{(1.08)^6}
* \frac{1}{(1.08)^7}
* \frac{1}{(1.08)^8}
* \frac{1}{(1.08)^9}
  \right]
  ]

If you actually plug those powers in and sum, you’ll again get:

[
P_0 \approx $1{,}835
]

---

## Method (b): Move each payment to year 9 (F), then back to year 0

1. Move each 500 at time (t) to year 9 using (F/P):

[
F_9 = \sum_{t=4}^{9} 500 \cdot (F/P, 8%, 9 - t)
= 500\left[
(1.08)^5 + (1.08)^4 + (1.08)^3 + (1.08)^2 + (1.08)^1 + (1.08)^0
\right]
]

2. Then discount that lump sum back 9 years:

[
P_0 = F_9 \cdot (P/F, 8%, 9)
]

Algebra collapses this to the same value as the other methods:

[
P_0 \approx $1{,}835
]

---

## Method (c): Use F/A at year 9, then discount to year 0

1. Treat it as a uniform series ending at year 9:

[
F_9 = 500 \cdot (F/A, 8%, 6)
= 500 \cdot 7.3359
\approx 3{,}667.96
]

2. Discount F₉ back 9 years:

[
P_0 = F_9 \cdot (P/F, 8%, 9)
= 3{,}667.96 \cdot 0.5002
\approx 1{,}835
]

Same again.

---

## Method (d) (already done, but in factor notation)

[
P_3 = 500(P/A, 8%, 6)
\approx 500 \cdot 4.6229 = 2{,}311.45
]

[
P_0 = P_3 (P/F, 8%, 3)
\approx 2{,}311.45 \cdot 0.7938 = 1{,}835
]

---

### Final numeric result (all methods):

[
\boxed{P_0 \approx $1{,}835}
]

If your test/solutions round differently, you might see something like $1,834.9 or $1,835.0 — same thing within rounding.

If you want to debug your own attempt, send me your intermediate numbers and we’ll see exactly where it drifted.

submissions.solution:
Let’s go straight through it and keep the logic tight.

### Step (a): NPV at 9%

Cash flows:

* Year 0: -50,000
* Year 1: +12,000
* Year 2: +16,000
* Year 3: +20,000
* Year 4: +8,000
* i = 9%

NPV:

[
NPV = -50{,}000 + \frac{12{,}000}{1.09} + \frac{16{,}000}{1.09^2} + \frac{20{,}000}{1.09^3} + \frac{8{,}000}{1.09^4}
]

Numerically:

* (12{,}000/1.09 \approx 11{,}009.17)
* (16{,}000/1.09^2 \approx 13{,}466.88)
* (20{,}000/1.09^3 \approx 15{,}443.67)
* (8{,}000/1.09^4 \approx 5{,}667.40)

Sum of discounted inflows:

[
PV_{\text{inflows}} \approx 11{,}009.17 + 13{,}466.88 + 15{,}443.67 + 5{,}667.40 \approx 45{,}587.13
]

So:

[
NPV = -50{,}000 + 45{,}587.13 \approx \boxed{-4{,}412.87}
]

(Project has **negative** NPV at 9%.)

In Excel style:

```excel
=NPV(0.09, 12000,16000,20000,8000) - 50000
```

---

### Step (b): Equivalent uniform annual amount (A) (years 1–4)

We want a **uniform net cash flow A in years 1–4** whose NPV equals the project’s NPV.

Use the capital recovery relation:

[
A = NPV \cdot (A/P, 9%, 4)
]

First compute ((A/P,9%,4)):

[
(A/P) = \frac{i(1+i)^n}{(1+i)^n - 1}
= \frac{0.09(1.09)^4}{(1.09)^4 - 1}
\approx 0.30867
]

Then:

[
A = -4{,}412.87 \times 0.30867 \approx \boxed{-1{,}362.12 \text{ per year}}
]

Spreadsheet-style with PMT, using the NPV as present value:

```excel
=PMT(0.09, 4, -4412.874506)
```

(You flip the sign inside PMT so that the result comes out negative, matching the fact that the project is a loser.)

---

### Final:

* **NPV at 9%:** ≈ **(-$4{,}412.87)**
* **Equivalent uniform annual amount (years 1–4):** ≈ **(-$1{,}362.12) per year**

Interpretation: the project is equivalent to *losing about $1.36k per year* over four years at a 9% MARR.

Good one to practice being precise.

### 1. Understand the cash flow

Years 1–7:

* Base: **150** every year
* Gradient (G = 50 starting in year 2):

  * Year 2: +50
  * Year 3: +100
  * Year 4: +150
  * Year 5: +200
  * Year 6: +250
  * Year 7: +300

So total per year:

| Year | Base | Gradient | Total |
| ---- | ---- | -------- | ----- |
| 1    | 150  | 0        | 150   |
| 2    | 150  | 50       | 200   |
| 3    | 150  | 100      | 250   |
| 4    | 150  | 150      | 300   |
| 5    | 150  | 200      | 350   |
| 6    | 150  | 250      | 400   |
| 7    | 150  | 300      | 450   |

Interest rate ( i = 12% ).

---

## 2. Present worth of base uniform series (P_{\text{base}})

Base is a uniform series: (A_{\text{base}} = 150), (n = 7).

[
P_{\text{base}} = A_{\text{base}} (P/A, 12%, 7)
= 150 \cdot \frac{1 - (1.12)^{-7}}{0.12}
]

Using ((P/A,12%,7) \approx 4.564):

[
P_{\text{base}} \approx 150 \cdot 4.564 \approx \boxed{684.6}
]

---

## 3. Present worth of gradient (P_G)

Standard arithmetic gradient: 0, 50, 100, …, 300 over years 1–7
(i.e. 6 gradient terms from year 2–7, so (n = 7) in the gradient formula).

Gradient factor:

[
P_G = G \cdot (P/G, 12%, 7)
= G \cdot \frac{(1+i)^n - i n - 1}{i^2 (1+i)^n}
]

With (i = 0.12), (n = 7), ((1.12)^7 \approx 2.2107):

* Numerator: (2.2107 - 0.12\cdot 7 - 1 \approx 0.3707)
* Denominator: (0.12^2 \cdot 2.2107 \approx 0.03183)

[
(P/G,12%,7) \approx \frac{0.3707}{0.03183} \approx 11.64
]

So:

[
P_G \approx 50 \cdot 11.64 \approx \boxed{582.2}
]

(check via direct discounting of the 50,100,…,300 terms — it matches).

---

## 4. Total present worth (P_T)

[
P_T = P_{\text{base}} + P_G
\approx 684.6 + 582.2 = \boxed{1{,}266.8}
]

---

## 5. Convert to annual series over 7 years

Use:

[
A = P \cdot (A/P, 12%, 7)
]

We already know (P/A \approx 4.564), so:

[
(A/P,12%,7) = \frac{1}{4.564} \approx 0.2191
]

### Base component (A_{\text{base}})

[
A_{\text{base}} = P_{\text{base}} (A/P,12%,7)
\approx 684.6 \cdot 0.2191 \approx \boxed{150}
]

(as expected – that’s a sanity check).

### Gradient component (A_G)

[
A_G = P_G (A/P,12%,7)
\approx 582.2 \cdot 0.2191 \approx \boxed{127.6}
]

### Total annual series (A_T)

[
A_T = A_{\text{base}} + A_G
\approx 150 + 127.6 = \boxed{277.6 \text{ per year}}
]

(You get the same if you do (A_T = P_T \cdot 0.2191).)

---

## Final neatly partitioned results

* ( \boxed{P_{\text{base}} \approx $684.6} )

* ( \boxed{P_G \approx $582.2} )

* ( \boxed{P_T \approx $1{,}266.8} )

* ( \boxed{A_{\text{base}} = $150 \text{/year}} )

* ( \boxed{A_G \approx $127.6 \text{/year}} )

* ( \boxed{A_T \approx $277.6 \text{/year}} )

If you want, we can reverse it and reconstruct each year’s cash flow from (A_T) to see the equivalence explicitly.
